q: A shelter clinician evaluates one-time 20 to 30 minute petting or play sessions to mitigate acute shelter stress. What is the physiological limitation of these short sessions?
o: Cortisol reductions occur during the session but do not persist an hour later, and multiple sessions add no further benefit
They trigger an immediate, dangerous surge in baseline heart rate
They induce permanent structural changes in the vomeronasal organ
Cortisol remains unaltered unless the volunteer is also reading aloud
e: The cortisol benefit of a short petting session is temporary (does not persist an hour later) and does not stack across multiple sessions.

q: A 15 minute petting session is implemented for newly admitted dogs. Which subpopulation will see a significant cortisol reduction from this single intervention?
o: Dogs surrendered directly by their owners
Dogs undergoing a 5-week medication washout
Dogs brought into the shelter as strays
Female dogs in novel pair housing
e: A 15 minute petting session lowered cortisol only in dogs admitted as strays, not in owner-relinquished dogs.

q: Which behavioural pattern in dogs returning from short foster stays is cited as cautiously optimistic evidence for foster?
o: More sedentary, avoided social contact, stopped yawning
Increased pica and stereotypic kennel pacing
More obedient, sought social interaction with handlers, responded readily to cues, jumped on strangers and barked less, yawned more
Elevated aggression at the kennel front toward unfamiliar dogs
e: Post-foster dogs showed improved obedience, more social initiative, fewer jumps on strangers, less barking, and more yawning.

q: In-kennel and out-of-kennel training programs were evaluated. What benefits and what consistency rule emerged?
o: Reduces pica; if training stops for 24 hours, door jumping returns to baseline
In-kennel training increases sitting, lying down, and quiet behaviour; out-of-kennel training reduces aggression. If training stops for 1 week, aggression returns to pre-intervention levels
Reduces barking by 142 times, but only via classical conditioning
Decreases locomotor activity only if performed for exactly 20 seconds
e: Training works in both contexts but is consistency-dependent; aggression rebounds after just 1 week of cessation.

q: In a 3-month, 211-dog group-housing study, what were the conflict and stereotypy outcomes?
o: Conflicts occurred daily and increased length of stay by 50%
Group housing caused a massive cortisol rise compared with novel solo housing
Stereotypies occurred at identical rates (10%) across solo and group housing
Only 5 incidents (light wounds) occurred; 10% of singly-housed dogs showed stereotypies while no group-housed dogs did
e: Group housing was safe (5 minor incidents over 3 months) and suppressed stereotypies (0% versus 10% in solo).

q: What fraction of a typical shelter dog population is generally suitable and available for daily off-leash interaction with other dogs?
o: Less than 1/3
More than 90% of the population
Exactly half
Only dogs in foster for 8 weeks
e: Fewer than one-third of typical shelter dogs are suitable and available for off-leash daily group interaction.

q: Which object did kenneled shelter dogs prefer over other in-kennel toy options?
o: A standard tennis ball
A soft squeaky plush bone
A robust Nylabone
A braided rope toy
e: In the kennel-toy preference study, dogs showed greater preference for the Nylabone over the other options.

q: When given a choice between robust and soft destructible toys, how did shelter dogs interact?
o: 100% interacted exclusively with robust toys for the whole session
Dogs spent the longest with a tennis ball and least with the squeaky bone
Robust toys completely prevented stereotypic pacing

Only about 35% interacted with the robust selections (averaging 2 minutes); more than 3/4 of dogs spent 25% of the 15 minute session on soft destructible toys, most time on squeaky bones and plushy toys, least time on the tennis ball
e: Most dogs preferred soft, destructible options (squeaky bone, plush) over robust toys, and the tennis ball was the least engaging soft option.

q: How did classical music compare with heavy metal in kenneled dogs?
o: Classical increased standing and vocalisation; heavy metal increased resting
Classical led to more resting, less standing, and more quiet behaviour; heavy metal increased body shaking, barking, and reduced resting
Heavy metal decreased barking frequency by 12 dB
Both genres produced an identical 30% drop in average barking amplitude
e: Classical functions as an acoustic sedative; heavy metal triggers shaking and barking and reduces rest.

q: A 2017 study tested five genres (classical, pop, soft rock, reggae, Motown) with shelter dogs. What happened during music and what happened immediately after it stopped?
o: Regardless of genre, dogs spent more time lying down and less time standing; however, dogs were 142 times more likely to bark after the music stopped
Dogs barked continuously during music but slept once it stopped
Reggae and Motown increased standing; classical and pop increased pacing
Barking frequency dropped during music and stayed low for an hour after
e: The Bowman 2017 five-genre study found all genres increased lying down during play, but a 142-fold spike in barking immediately followed the music stopping.

q: Which essential oil scents are sedating, and which are stimulating, in scented-cloth studies?
o: Peppermint and rosemary are sedating; lavender and chamomile are stimulating
Valerian and ginger are stimulating; coconut and peppermint are sedating
All scents increase resting equally compared with a no-cloth control
Lavender, chamomile, coconut, and ginger are sedating; rosemary and peppermint are stimulating
e: Per the scented-cloth study data, lavender, chamomile, coconut, and ginger are sedating; rosemary and peppermint are stimulating.

q: A behaviour department installs DAP (dog appeasing pheromone) diffusers. What specific impact on barking is documented?
o: DAP eliminates peak barking amplitude entirely
DAP reduced average barking AMPLITUDE by about 30%; barking FREQUENCY and PEAK amplitude did not differ from placebo
DAP made dogs 142 times less likely to bark after environmental noise
DAP increased barking frequency but lowered heart rate
e: DAP cuts the average loudness by about 30% but does not reduce peak amplitude or barking frequency.

q: What operational rule determines whether to MODIFY a broader enrichment STRATEGY?
o: Wait exactly 2 months before any programmatic changes
If no positive behavioural change occurs within 1 week at most, modify the strategy
Modify the strategy every 15 minutes to prevent rapid habituation
Modify only if peak barking amplitude rises by 12 dB
e: If the strategy fails to produce positive behavioural change within 1 week at most, modify it.

q: Which measurement method involves quickly assessing many animals by focusing on one dog for an instant, recording what it is doing in that moment, then immediately shifting to the next dog?
o: Continuous measurement
Permanent products
Instantaneous scan sampling (ISS)
Interval recording
e: ISS lets one observer cover many dogs by recording behaviour for an instant per animal and then moving on.

q: What is the principal operational benefit of the PERMANENT PRODUCTS method?
o: Real-time precise data on canine heart-rate variability
The observer can record tangible outcomes (chewed toys, urine and faeces, emptied KONGs) at their convenience, without being present when the behaviour occurs
It removes the need to rotate classical music compilations
It is the only method that captures subtle changes in peak barking amplitude
e: Permanent products allow asynchronous recording of tangible behavioural traces, which is operationally practical for staff.

q: Under standard shelter guidelines, how is feline enrichment defined and prioritised?
o: As social interaction, physical and mental stimulation, opportunities for species-typical behaviours, and choice and control, given the same significance as nutrition and medical care and never optional
As an optional add-on provided only when staffing allows
As a purely physical concept limited to cage size
As something needed only for cats staying longer than 2 weeks
e: The ASV defines enrichment by these four pillars and treats it as a required, never-optional component of care.

q: What are the stated goals of a feline enrichment programme?
o: To increase length of stay so cats habituate fully
To replace medical care with behavioural care
To increase behavioural diversity and normal behaviour, reduce abnormal behaviour, increase positive use of the environment, and improve coping
To minimise all human contact to reduce disease
e: Feline enrichment aims to broaden normal behaviour, cut abnormal behaviour, and improve environmental use and coping.

q: How does the duration of daily human interaction affect the Cat Stress Score (CSS) in shelter cats?
o: 60 minutes per day reduced CSS from day 1 to day 2, while 20 minutes per day did not
20 minutes per day reduced CSS but 60 minutes increased it
Neither duration changed CSS
Only physical restraint changed CSS
e: The longer 60-minute daily interaction lowered CSS within a day, whereas the standard 20-minute interaction did not.

q: A shelter cat is not accustomed to close physical contact with people. What interaction style does the source recommend?
o: Immediate full-body restraint to build tolerance
Marathon petting along the back to the tail base
No interaction at all until adoption
Interaction via a toy or treat, or a person sitting nearby and reading aloud, rather than forced physical contact
e: Cats less used to people often do better with indirect, low-pressure contact (toy, treat, or a person reading nearby).

q: According to ASV guidance, how should social contact be tailored for poorly socialised animals?
o: All animals benefit equally from forced human handling
Poorly socialised adults should be handled intensively until they comply
Poorly socialised animals may not benefit from human contact, except young puppies and kittens, but may find comfort with their own species
Social isolation is preferable for poorly socialised animals
e: ASV notes social isolation is profoundly negative; poorly socialised adults may take comfort from conspecifics rather than people, with young kittens the exception.

q: How do appropriately group-housed cats compare with singly housed cats?
o: They show more locomotion and social or solitary play and tend toward a lower cortisol-to-creatinine ratio
They show higher cortisol and more stereotypy
They stop eating and hide permanently
They show no measurable difference
e: With adequate space, group-housed cats are more active and playful and tend toward a lower cortisol-to-creatinine ratio.

q: When is interspecies (dog and cat) cohousing considered acceptable in the source?
o: Whenever kennel space is limited
To socialise feral cats to dogs
Routinely, to save housing space
Not recommended, unless a dog and cat were surrendered together and are reported to be bonded
e: Cross-species cohousing is discouraged except for an already-bonded dog and cat surrendered together.

q: What does the evidence show about feline toy preference and use?
o: Cats play longer with interactive (human-moved) toys than solo-play toys, and toys should be rotated daily
Cats prefer solo toys and ignore human-moved toys
Cats never engage with toys in a shelter
A single toy left indefinitely maintains interest best
e: Human-moved interactive toys simulate prey and hold attention longer; daily rotation counters habituation.

q: Frustrated shelter cats received four 10-minute training sessions per day for 10 days. What outcomes were documented?
o: A spike in cortisol and more upper respiratory disease
No measurable change versus controls
More positive mood, higher secretory IgA, and a lower likelihood of developing feline upper respiratory infection
Complete loss of appetite and withdrawal
e: Cognitive engagement through short daily training improved mood and mucosal immunity (S-IgA) and reduced FURI in frustrated cats.

q: How do cats respond to silvervine compared with catnip?
o: Catnip produces a response in 100% of cats; silvervine in none
Both produce identical responses in exactly half of cats
Neither has any behavioural effect on cats
About 79% of cats respond to silvervine versus about 68% to catnip, and the response intensity to silvervine is significantly greater
e: Silvervine reaches more cats than catnip and elicits a stronger response, useful for cats that do not respond to catnip.

q: What is documented about visual enrichment for shelter cats?
o: Cats attend most to moving or linear images but lose interest over time, and with window access 89% spent 1 to 5 hours a day at the window
Cats watch screens for most of the day indefinitely
Static images hold attention better than motion
Cats show no interest in windows
e: Motion draws feline attention but wanes; window access is highly used, with most cats spending 1 to 5 hours a day observing.

q: What does ASV guidance emphasise about auditory enrichment in cat housing?
o: Loud music at all times maximises calm
Any genre at high volume is beneficial
Species-specific music for cats can reduce stress, but reducing excess noise may matter more than adding sound
Silence is harmful and must always be avoided
e: Cat-specific music can help, yet ASV stresses that cutting excess noise is often more valuable than adding sound.

q: What caveat does ASV note about pheromone products (for example Feliway) used for enrichment?
o: They work instantly and replace all other enrichment
They are effective only in dogs
They should never be used in shelters
They are less likely to be effective without a comprehensive stress-reduction and enrichment plan
e: ASV: pheromones are unlikely to help much unless embedded in a broader enrichment and stress-reduction plan.

q: What are the key principles for socialising kittens in the shelter?
o: Isolate each kitten individually from birth to prevent disease
Socialise between 2 and 7 weeks of age, house with littermates and the queen until weaning, and aim for 20 to 30 minutes of daily handling by a variety of people
Begin socialisation only after 16 weeks of age
Limit handling to a single caretaker for the first 8 weeks
e: The sensitive period (about 2 to 7 weeks), littermate and queen contact, and varied gentle handling underpin normal kitten development.

q: A high-energy shelter cat shows persistent meowing, reaching through the bars, pacing, and reduced grooming with growing inappetence. How should this be interpreted and managed?
o: As normal contentment requiring no action
As chronic frustration from under-stimulation progressing toward depression, which must be treated as a welfare emergency
As a sign the cat should be isolated in a dark room
As status aggression requiring a startle stimulus
e: Under-stimulation in high-energy cats causes frustration that can deteriorate into depression, a welfare emergency needing prompt enrichment and assessment.
